title: The Birthday Problem
objective: After this level you can explain why 23 people are enough for a better than even chance that two share a birthday.
summary: In a group of 23 people, the chance two share a birthday is 50.7%. The trick is counting pairs (253 of them) and working out the chance that nobody matches.

cards.headline: 23 people in a room. Better than even odds that two share a birthday.
cards.body: It sounds far too few. There are 365 days to choose from, after all. Yet with just 23 people, a shared birthday is more likely than not. The secret is in what you're counting.

cards.headline: Count pairs, not people
cards.body: The usual mistake is thinking about your own birthday. The question is whether any two people match, and 23 people make 253 different pairs: the first person pairs with 22 others, the next with 21 more, and so on down to 1. Each pair is a fresh chance for a match. With 253 chances, a match stops sounding strange.

cards.headline: Level 24's trick does the math
cards.body: It's easier to find the chance that nobody matches. The second person misses the first one's birthday 364 times in 365. The third must miss both: 363 in 365. Keep multiplying, one person at a time. By the 23rd person, the chance of no match has sunk just below half, so the chance of at least one match is 50.7%.

cards.fact: At 57 people, a match is about 99% certain.
cards.context: The chance climbs fast because pairs grow much faster than people: 23 people make 253 pairs, but 57 people make 1,596. The math assumes birthdays are spread evenly over 365 days and leaves out leap years. Real births aren't perfectly even, but the difference this makes is negligible.
